short: the number a relation's files are named after. TRUNCATE and VACUUM FULL give a table a new one; its oid stays.
one of a relation's files, told apart by suffix: main (the pages), _fsm, _vm, and _init for unlogged tables.
a relation's files are cut into 1 GB pieces: 16486, 16486.1, 16486.2. each holds 131,072 pages.
a 4-byte slot near the top of a page holding a tuple's offset, length and flags. the second number in a ctid.
the first 24 bytes of every page: its LSN, checksum, flags, pd_lower, pd_upper, pd_special and prune xid.
bytes at the end of a page kept for the access method. heap pages leave it empty, b-tree pages keep sibling links there.
the extension that reads raw pages: page_header(), heap_page_items(), bt_page_items() and friends.
the 23 bytes at the start of every heap tuple: xmin, xmax, cid, ctid, two flag words and t_hoff.
one bit per column after the tuple header, present only when the row has a NULL. a NULL takes no other space.
empty bytes before a column so it starts at a multiple of its type's alignment (typalign: 1, 2, 4 or 8).
how postgres stores values over about 2 KB: compressed first, then cut into chunks in a side table, with a pointer left in the row.
the 18 bytes left in a row in place of a value moved out to the toast table.
a fork that records roughly how much room each page has, as a tree of max values, so inserts find space fast.
a fork with two bits per page, all-visible and all-frozen. vacuum and index-only scans use it to skip pages.
how full an INSERT packs a page. lower than 100 leaves room so updates can stay on the same page.
the shared hash table that maps a page (relation, fork, block) to the buffer frame holding it.
a backend's claim on a buffer while it uses the page. a pinned buffer can't be evicted.
the extension that lists every buffer frame: which page it holds, its usage count, and whether it's dirty or pinned.
a counter from 0 to 5 on each buffer, raised by every pin and lowered by each pass of the clock hand.
postgres's buffer replacement: a hand goes round the frames, lowering usage counts, and evicts the first one at zero.
a small private set of buffers a big seq scan, VACUUM or bulk write recycles, so it doesn't evict everyone's pages.
a page in shared buffers that has changed since it was last written to its file. normal, not an error.
the process that writes dirty buffers just ahead of the clock hand, so backends rarely have to.
the process that writes every dirty buffer for a checkpoint, then fsyncs the files.
the same page cached twice: in shared buffers and in the operating system's page cache under it.
postgres 18's setting for who performs asynchronous reads: worker (the default), io_uring, or sync.
code that knows which blocks it will read next, so it can ask early, combine neighbours and keep several reads in flight.
